title: Draft: wsdb: Export as wsdb (wireshark database) format
description:
Packet details can be exported as wsdb (wireshark database).
A wsdb file a sqlite based database which stores the entire packet data and the complete dissection tree including reassembled buffers. It is the intention to have a file format to persist dissection results while having the data in a structured way that they can be accessed quickly and easily even when for giant files. (sqlite database tools or libraries)

To optimize export performance it implemented with a double buffered queue (dissection thread and n commit threads) and can ba parallelized to use all available cores. In case of a parallelized export the output is splitted into n files while n is the number of cores -1. These files can be aggregated easily in different ways (e.g. Sqlite command ATTACH or opening multiple database connections).

To improve export performance even further the sqlite journal and disk synchronization is switched off.

To optimize file size unique strings are stored in dedicated table to prevent duplicates.

Field values are encoded as an integer, a double or string value. They may have an additional representation value which is typically a calculated string to display in the GUI.

Export can be accessed via GUI (File -> Export Packet Dissection).

A GUI tool called wsdb_browser can be used to browse wsdb files. It is on basic prototype level right now but it is able the aggregate splitted wsdb files.

What does -dev mean?
Wireshark mailing list developer https://www.wireshark.org/lists/
Shall I create an additional issue for this MR?
No, it is a big chance, i will be nice to talk on -dev mailing

As @alagoutte mentioned, there should have been a discussion initiated on -dev about the inclusion for sqlite3. Nothing happend in that regard. The only path forward for me is to handle this library the same way we do every other where it may have security implications - not include directly but rather have it available on the build system.

One more thing. You changed the header of sqlite3.h to reflect the Wireshark license. Never, ever do this. This is legally not sound or valid and code will not be permitted that sails under a different license, except where it had been extensively modified to do so. Here that is not the case.

  • 83e4d6ab - wsdb: Export as wsdb (wireshark database) format
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/3903/diffs?diff_id=233230234&start_sha=3210ec3c700e68ec920ed29f5c98387b98feec60)

What is the advantage in using this approach over exporting a dissection result as separate pcapng file (together with annotation that might include a reference to the original file and filter used)? I am currently a little bit confused, what the big advantage would be to utilize a different format, when you can just export the dissected file and reopen it as a subset?

The idea was basically born in this discussion: #17468 
Originally the idea was that it might be beneficial to have the dissection result in a structured format as sqlite file to be able to perform filtering and sorting in a faster way later on.

But honestly it did not work out very well for this purpose. Even the time that the export requires makes it uninteresting for this purpose. (Caused by the fact that dissection adds so many infomation to the packet itself that the dissection result becomes bigger by a factor of 100 easily compared to the originaly pcapng file.)

For the performance improvement I think #17547 would have a much bigger impact.

**Nevertheless**: Compared to an export as PDML it has some interesting advantages. If you are on a machine with many cores the export time is significantly less and you access subsets of the the exported data way easier compared to a large XML file which always needs to be consumed as a whole. That is a big benefit since these exports become quite big and parsing the file as a wholes requires a lot of memory.

Another benefit could be if you want to share the dissection of packets with someone who does not have the same set of plugins and dissectors (lua) as you do.

Another benefit that I see that you make the dissection result accessable to other application an scripts because sqlite is basically useable in any environment.

**Question:**
> What is the advantage in using this approach over exporting a dissection result as separate pcapng file (together with annotation that might include a reference to the original file and filter used)?

How do you export a pcapng file including the dissection trees?

> Another benefit that I see that you make the dissection result accessable to other application an scripts because sqlite is basically useable in any environment.

That was exactly my first thought when I saw this MR and I intend to give it a try as soon as I can.
At work, we do have a need to export some very precise statistics about what is going on on the network regarding some communications that cover several layers: TCP->TLS->Thrift->Internal->Additional

* The first 3 are already fully covered by Wireshark.
* The "Internal" layer will be covered by a sub-dissector based on the Thrift one, therefore by Wireshark (low maintenance if I can generate this sub-dissector automatically).
* The "Additional" layer is mostly about decoding some binary blobs inside that.

Until now, the idea was to implement some kind of plugin inside Wireshark that would export the data in a suitable format for us but this approach looks very heavy on the implementation and maintenance side (not a lot of C developers and unlikely to have time to work on this project due to priorities).

With this export in a common database format, we would be able to push the data analysis to other developers that are more common in-house (C#, Python, C++, PowerShell, … YMMV) and the independence from a specific Wireshark build would also help split independent task (no more bottleneck on the export side).

Edit: I took a look at a PDML (I didn’t know about that export until this post, thanks), and I still think the sqlite3 export would be a great addition and a better option for some use case, especially with the number of optimized libraries for this database format.
Maybe you might find [shark_x](https://gitlab.com/Developer-Alexander/shark_x/-/tree/v0.2.0) helpful as it allows you to extend Wireshark with python or javascript scripts.

So basically you want to have a direct API interface masquerading as data-export. Again, something we could do with JSON already. And there is a good reason for not exporting the dissection trees, as those change from version to version. 

But I can see why this is useful in some usecases (as mentioned above). Therefore I can resolve this thread for me.
How shall we proceed?

I still am not 100% convinced that we should include it, but I do not see a negative outcome going forward at this point. I think it can be a useful addition. But for that, a few things have to apply, which are not yet being done:

1. Bundling the sqlite3 source with Wireshark is a very bad idea. We would need to follow the changes on their end to especially monitor security related issues. Therefore the library should be included via the official sqlite3 repos, not directly (Obviously this contradicts somewhat @alagoutte response in https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/3903#note_657948995 . But it is the more sensible solution to not include sqlite3 into the sourcecode.
2. Building with wsdb support should be optional, similar to HAVE_EXTCAP or HAVE_MINIZIP is. The reason for that is, that some people may not wish to integrate support or want to build lighter versions of Wireshark for internal use. Default can be to build it for now.
3. I would add the entry for wsdb more towards the end of the list. For one, it is a new addition, and two some people may have auto-scripted Wiresharks UI and therefore would require changes to that
4. You have added command-line options to tshark & Co, but not to Wireshark itself. Not really a blocker, but it would make sense if those are added as well.
Third party libraries should be detected via CMake and integrated as such. You can use minizip as an example, on how such a detection works.
What is the basis for this calculation? Please add a comment explaining it.

What about packets that dont have source or destination? A lot of fields feel duplicated to suit a very narrow usecase (although a usecase utilized by a majority of users). But Wireshark can dissect more protocols than just Ethernet based, and for those this struct might not apply. I would also strive to reuse as much as the already present information as possibel, to avoid further modification if things change
This will get outdated, everytime there is the slightest change in epan.

We purposefully try to avoid non wmem-based memory as much as we can. This memory operation is not safe, unless the pointer uses the same pool as the original pointer did, and even than it is not guaranteed to have the data at the point of calling. This is very very dangerous for memory work

Your "claim" is, to present more information than the existing data export tools, when in reality you actually use a very narrow subset and just dump additional data to let others find it. You also claim, that other export formats do not present the tree, when in reality you do neither (at least not fully). And your export will run very very costly, both memory and time-consuming wise, due to numerous sub-selects, instead of handling that in c-code where it is much faster and the data already available.

You just assume here, that no field is presented twice in the tree, when in reality that happens all-the-time. You cannot ensure, that you will only see a field id or name once, how are you ensuring that those fields get added to the correct tree?
why? Where is that documented
again, use wmem
field id is never unique, nor is name
The timestamp accuracy is dependant on the capture and settings. None of which are queried here

The packet length is only half the answer, as there is a captured length. For instance a packet may report a length of 500 bytes but only 64 bytes got captured. This is not reflected in your code, but a very useful capture still

Ok, now you are just asking to be lied to. This column contains the last source added to it. Which can be vastly different than the src of the packet. But you put it in the main packet_data as truth?

For instance, IP ov. IP may carry multiple IP packets. The SRC column will than carry also multiple entries, neither of which is the source of the packet, as that had been overwritten.

Same goes for protocol btw, and info.
Possible memory leak. Although you "fail" here, still stuff in the g_hash_table's may be freed. That's why you use wmem

Why not always utilize multicore? Is there a reason for explicitly having it single-core? The user will always use the first version, just because it is found first.

Just make it always multicore and add a preference to turn that off if so desired by the user
This should be underneath tools, not in main
marked this merge request as **draft**
Marking this change as Draft, as it needs some work before it is merge-ready

I thank you very much for your extensive feedback. I appreciate it very much.

I will close this MR anyway because some of the requested changes are out of my reach.

This specifically affects the inclusion of sqlite as a library in the build process. And I obviously don't know all the possibilities and combinations of packets and fields that Wireshark covers.

However, I do believe that the idea has potential.

Hi

I appreciate your answer and honesty. May I offer one piece of advice though? I have 25+ years of coding experience and can say with some levels of confidence, that your code was sound and good. Rather than seeing the task as too huge, you could also see it as an opportunity to learn and improve. My first huge contribution to Wireshark took nearly 100 comments back and forth and lasted about 4 months. And by the end, not only was the code way more stable and better suited, but also I learned a ton of stuff that I still apply every day.

I see, that you are very enthusiastic about this, so don't give up. Polish it and come back. We will always gladly offer advice and guidance to help you through the process. That is what open-source is all about after all. If our reviews sometimes feel a little bit strict or harsh at first, believe me, that is only because we've been there and we just know how high the mountain can be sometimes and honesty is a better guide than false amplification.

Although I do not see the full potential of the idea - just because it is not something I require in my daily work (maybe - yet?) - I see your enthusiasm about it. That alone would be enough motivation for me to help you get it to fruition.

So, in summary, we are here and whenever you decide to pick up this idea again, we will help you through it.

kind regards
Roland

Thank you for your advise. I did like to hear it.

This feature relies on sqlite. For me there are two different way to include sqlite:
1. Add sqlite amalgamation to the source and use it
2. Include sqlite as a prebuild lib to the project (comparable to lua or others)

Which option do you think is the better one? 

Option 2 is something that I could not do by myself. That is something that I need help with. In this case it may be a good idea to split things up. In first step make sqlite availible as a lib within the project and add the code that is using sqlite in a second step.

My overall intention was to find a way to speed up querying the dissection result. The basic idea was to dissect once and query many times afterwards. The export to an sqlite data based seemed to be a way to do so as sqlite can be very good for querying data. (if done properly)

I would like to know your opinion on the general use case to speed up querying the dissection result by some kind of caching or exporting dissection results. Maybe there are already existing solutions that I just do not know of.

Would we really need sqlite ourselves? Would not a pre-built version of sqlite suffice? For instance, it is available via chocolatey (https://community.chocolatey.org/packages/SQLite) in version 3.9.3 atm. Same goes for macOS with brew and Linux. So that would be the distribution path.

Now, the more pressing matter would be to make it available in the build system. For that, FindSqlite3 can be used (https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/FindSQLite3.html) which is part of cmake since 3.14. Checking with our CMakeLists.txt file shows, that the minimum version for Wireshark in cmake is 3.10 on Linux/macOS and 3.13 on Windows. Now, we are currently pumping up a lot of versions, so it may be feasible to pump cmake to 3.14 across the platform. Alternatively the feature simply would only be available on those systems where cmake checks reveal a version 3.14 or higher. That should be easily be achieved with a few checks in cmake. Personally I would go down that route, even if it means that some older systems do not have this feature available to them, because most users would have a cmake version > 3.14 installed anyway and would not register an issue.

After getting that solved, the main source code should be guarded to build only if sqlite has actually been found. That would be done by guarding all calls in the general code with HAVE_SQLITE3 and preventing the inclusion of the wsdb files in the corresponding CMakeFiles. Examples how that has been done can be found by looking for ENABLE_EXTCAP or HAVE_MINIZIP. 

Lastly, I would include an option in CMakeOptions.txt to disable the functionality by default (ENABLE_WSDB OFF) and only enable it if required. My personal guess will be, that this functionality will be used by in-house builds of Wireshark mostly, and not by general available builds. Also, this reduces the risk of breaking functionality, if someone updates a version and some internal stuff had changed.

In general, the day-to-day user will not be using this functionality. Most users are plenty satisfied with the speed they currently have for filtering. It also comes down - very heavily - to how users approach dissection in general. If you follow popular online tutorials for instance by Chris Greer (@packethead), you will see, that when they start a new dissection, the first thing they initially do is drill down on the issue with very little functionality enabled. The closer they get, the more features they enable, but also the pcap files get more specific and smaller. So speed is not really an issue here. 

I can see a use-case in automatic testing scenarios or in-house builds, where the interface is being used to enable testing and surveillance of a device behavior. Even in IDS systems it can be useful to search for certain attack vectors or scenarios automatically. But in those cases you do not need to have it enabled by default, as most commonly those are special-build versions of Wireshark with just the features enabled, that they require (in most cases for instance, EXTCAP is disabled to save a lot of space and boot-up time)

I agree to make this feature optional.

For windows would you require sqlite3 being installed globally on the machine? Or would you do it like it is done for lua which is downloaded during cmake configuration?

I am targeting use cases with automatic testing and and IDS like features. But the issue with this is that the company I am working for does not deal with custom build. I am restricted to official builds. And my assumption would be that the majority of users is working with the official builds.

> Most users are plenty satisfied with the speed they currently have for filtering.

How do you know?

Especially when using with dissectors written in lua speed can become an issue very quickly.

> the first thing they initially do is drill down on the issue with very little functionality enabled. The closer they get, the more features they enable, but also the pcap files get more specific and smaller. So speed is not really an issue here.

I agree this is the best way to go. This is what I do all the time. But you could also read this as a _workaround_ that every user needs to do every time to get the job done in time.
